targetText: Every change in the social order, every revolution in property relations, is the necessary consequence of the creation of new forces of production which no longer fit into the old property relations.
summary: Every transformation in property relations is the necessary consequence of new productive forces outgrowing the old social order.
explanation: Engels states the foundational law of historical materialism: property forms and legal systems do not change arbitrarily through moral decrees, but because expanding technological and economic capacities no longer fit inside outmoded social structures.

targetText: When, towards the end of the Middle Ages, there arose a new mode of production which could not be carried on under the then existing feudal and guild forms of property, this new mode of production, which had outgrown the old property relations, created a new property form; private property.
summary: The rise of manufacturing at the end of the Middle Ages outgrew feudal guild restrictions, creating the modern capitalist property form.
explanation: Engels illustrates the historical progression of modes of production: when manufacturing techniques developed beyond medieval guild limits, feudal land relations were broken and replaced by bourgeois private property as the only system capable of organizing the new productive forces.

targetText: The agrarian Middle Ages give us the baron and the serf; the cities of the Later Middle Ages show us the guildmaster and the journeyman and the day laborer; the 17th century has its manufacturing workers; the 19th has big factory owners and proletarians.
summary: The class structure of society evolves across historical epochs, from feudal serfdom to guild workshops, manufacture, and modern industrial capitalism.
explanation: Marxism traces class divisions to specific stages of production: the feudal mode generated lords and serfs; commercial urban centers generated masters and journeymen; and modern mechanized industry divides society into the bourgeoisie and the wage-earning proletariat.

targetText: Now, under these conditions, the abolition of private property has become not only possible but absolutely necessary.
summary: Because modern industrial forces now outgrow private corporate ownership, transitioning from capitalism to socialism is historically necessary.
explanation: Just as feudalism was overthrown when it constrained manufacturing, capitalism now constrains automated mass production through recurring crises and poverty amidst abundance, making the transition to common socialist ownership a historical necessity.
